1.pericope_label: O Lord, thou hast searched me, and known me: such knowledge is too wonderful for me

schools.summary: Augustine assigns the psalm to Christ speaking in prophecy, sometimes in his own name and sometimes in ours, so that what is said in the person of the flesh he took belongs to the ascended head and to the members still toiling.

Calvin assumes David wrote it and canvasses the winnowing verb through several older versions and critics; his block also carries a later paragraph reporting the authorship quarrel and rebutting it. Gill reports the reading thou hast formed me but keeps besetting, taking it of the presence and providence that nothing escapes.

Spurgeon takes the searching as thorough as an officer searching for contraband or a plunderer ransacking a house, but warns the figure must not run on all fours since searching implies an ignorance God has not; Henry reads the sifting morally as separating corn from chaff and hears a physician feeling a pulse in the laid hand.

Clarke argues from Chaldaisms that the psalm is not David’s but belongs to the captivity or later, renders the disputed verb winnow or sift, and follows an emendation joining two verses to give thou hast formed me; Wesley reads the same verb as a siege metaphor, of soldiers setting watches round about.

Ellicott notes Aramaic forms found nowhere else, finds the received rendering of the third verse founded on a mistaken etymology and prefers a verb meaning to lodge, giving the sense that God is a guest about the path and bed; Keil and Delitzsch hold the psalm composed after the Davidic model rather than by David, yet worthy of him.

debates: Did David write this psalm? Clarke says the internal evidence of several Chaldaisms puts it in or after the captivity and leaves the author unknown, though the composition is worthy of David; Keil and Delitzsch hold it inscribed to David because composed after his model; Ellicott points to Aramaic forms found nowhere else; and Calvin, who assumes David throughout, is followed by a paragraph that names Clarke and answers that the Chaldaisms are merely one letter mistaken for another by a transcriber used to that idiom.

What does the verb rendered compassest mean? Clarke and Calvin read winnow, ventilate or sift, and Henry takes it morally as separating corn from chaff; Ellicott holds the received rendering to rest on a mistaken etymology and prefers a verb meaning to lodge, so that God is a guest about the path and bed; Wesley reads it as a siege, of soldiers setting watches round about their enemies.

Is the next verse besetting or forming? Gill reports the rendering thou hast formed me, urged of the formation of the body, but keeps besetting; Clarke adopts the other and joins two verses to get it; Ellicott reads the word of a beleaguered city from which there is no escape.
outliers: Ellicott illustrates the word for thought, which he derives from a root meaning companion, by a line of Macbeth about keeping alone and making companions of the sorriest fancies.
Calvin reports an archbishop objecting that winnowing would sound uncouth, and a bishop supposing the metaphor to be taken from hunting.
Henry remarks that divine truths look fully as well when they are prayed over as when they are preached over, and much better than when they are disputed over.
themes: omniscience acknowledged in the second person rather than argued
a disputed title and a disputed date
one verb read as winnowing, lodging and besieging
the body formed and the man beset
knowledge confessed too high to be attained

7.pericope_label: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? if I ascend up into heaven, thou art there

schools.summary: Spurgeon observes that the psalmist gets no answer to his question but its own echo, and presses the consequence that sin is committed to God’s face at the foot of his throne; Henry derives the omniscience from the omnipresence and cites a heathen saying that whichever way you turn you will see God meeting you.

Gill canvasses wind, God himself, and the divine mind as senses of the word spirit before settling on the third Person, calls the ascent a hyperbolical expression, and reads the leading hand of the tenth verse as the grace that guides a saint like a parent teaching a child to walk.

Clarke insists the word cannot mean breath or wind, notes that the second clause is literally from thy faces and asks whether the plural intends the persons of the Godhead, distributes the presence by attribute through heaven and hell and earth, and turns from the darkness verse into open polemic against the doctrine of reprobation; Wesley reads the flight as east to west, the sea standing for the western border.

Ellicott traces the spirit clause forward to the words spoken to the woman of Samaria, admires the wings of the morning as the swift sailing of light across the world, finds an advance of thought in the underworld not being exempt from God’s visitation, and proposes then withdraws a rendering of the darkness clause as crushing; Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition from omnipresence to the origin of man.

debates: What is the spirit from which no flight escapes? Gill runs through the wind, God himself as Spirit, and the divine mind before preferring the third Person; Clarke rules out breath and wind as making the passage ridiculous and reads the plural faces of the following clause as evidence for the persons of the Godhead; Ellicott holds that the clause alone would mean creative and providential power but that its parallel with presence reaches toward what was later said to the woman of Samaria.

How should the darkness clause be rendered? Gill and Clarke take it plainly of a man supposing night will hide what he does; Ellicott proposes let darkness crush me, noting the older versions kept the metaphor and that commentators have mostly been frightened of it, then argues himself back to the received sense on the ground that the passage needs a place of concealment rather than an assault.
outliers: Clarke breaks off his note on the darkness into a direct attack on the doctrine of reprobation, refusing to make the fountain of eternal love a streamlet of capricious love to thousands and a tide of hatred to millions, and answering the objection that nobody holds such doctrines by saying that then he has written against nobody.

Ellicott observes that the psalmist here speaks as though he were a guilty being trying to escape notice, and draws from it that when God overtakes those who hide from him it is to take them under his care.
Gill notes that the heathens also represented the morning as having wings.
themes: omnipresence argued as the ground of omniscience
a question answered only by its own echo
height, depth, distance and darkness exhausted in turn
the underworld brought inside the divine vigilance
a commentator quarrelling with his own proposed reading

13.pericope_label: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: how precious also are thy thoughts unto me

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes God not merely the observer but the owner of the inmost parts, as much at home there as a landlord on his own estate, and says the psalmist was hidden away as a treasure before he could know anything; Henry orders the divine counsels under three heads as precious, numerous and constant.

Gill reads the substance as the bones and the unformed mass as a bottom of yarn wound up, notes that heathen physicians were astonished at the structure of the body, and meets the numbering of the sand with a long run of ancient poets, oracles and mathematicians who boasted of counting it.

Clarke assembles the needlework reading from two other writers, reads fearfully as pointing to the frailty of a body the slightest accident may destroy, keeps the received reading of the sixteenth verse and extends the embroidery figure to the pattern before the workman, and declines to enter minutely into anatomical detail out of deference to the delicacy of the text; Wesley reads the book as the counsel and providence that contrived the work.

Ellicott confirms the tapestry figure from the tabernacle passages but leaves weaving and embroidery undecided, renders fearfully as separated or distinguished and offers a national sense, holds the received reading of the sixteenth verse improbable and refers the pronoun to the days, and hears dreams continued into waking in the last clause; Keil and Delitzsch derive the word for the embryo from a root meaning to wrap together and cite its use of raw material awaiting the workman.

debates: Whose members, or whose days, are written in the book? Clarke keeps the received reading and builds the embroidery figure on it, quoting a writer who compares the pattern kept before an embroiderer; Ellicott holds that supplying the word members gives a possible but not a probable sense, refers the pronoun to the days instead, sets out two renderings word for word, and prefers a slight change yielding that the days are all reckoned and not one of them wanting.

What does fearfully mean here? Clarke takes it of frailty, since the texture of the body is so delicate that the slightest accident may destroy a part essential to life, and holds that God made us so to teach us to walk with death while keeping life in view; Ellicott renders the word separated or distinguished, either of being separated from the womb and so born, or, if the reference is national, of one nation chosen in distinction from other races.
outliers: Clarke quotes a writer who observes that the most artful needlework was by law dedicated to the sanctuary, in the high priest’s dress and the curtains of the tabernacle, so that the making of the body is compared to the finest work men made for God.

Gill answers the sand with a catalogue: a poet who said sand flies number, an oracle that boasted of knowing the number of the sand and the measures of the sea, a mathematician derided by a satirist as the measurer of earth and sea and of the sand without number, and a geometer whose book proving the sand not infinite is still extant.
Ellicott rejects the reading that makes the rolled thing a ball of the threads of destiny, on the ground that this is not a Hebrew conception.
Clarke says the subject might have been illustrated much more particularly, but that the delicacy of expression in the text teaches him to avoid entering too minutely into anatomical detail.
themes: the body made as needlework dedicated to the sanctuary
an unformed mass compared to raw material awaiting the workman
a book of members or a book of days
wonder and frailty heard in the same word
thoughts too many to be numbered

19.pericope_label: Surely thou wilt slay the wicked, O God: search me, O God, and know my heart

schools.summary: Spurgeon draws the punishment straight out of the omniscience already established, since crimes committed before the face of the judge cannot go unpunished, and reads the dismissal of the men of blood as the psalmist refusing his own company to those God has refused his.

Gill observes that the word for the wicked is singular, reports a rabbinic reading that referred it to Esau and so to the Christians, and defends the hatred by narrowing it to men as haters of God and to their works rather than their persons.

Clarke holds the closing verses a fragment of some other psalm, rejects a bishop’s rendering of the twentieth verse and prefers one about seizing cities, abhors the conduct rather than the men, observes that the closing prayer was needed precisely because of the hatred just expressed, and reads the last phrase as the old way of the fathers; Wesley dismisses the hatred in one line as the Jewish rather than the Christian spirit.

Ellicott grants the abruptness but explains it from the Hebrew temper, which turned indignation on concrete sin where a modern would speculate on the origin of evil, calls the text of the twentieth verse unsatisfactory and canvasses emendations and Greek renderings, and holds the closing word to mean the ancient and therefore the true religion; Keil and Delitzsch supply the transition and note that the searching confessed at the opening is here entreated.

debates: Do these verses belong to this psalm? Clarke says they have no visible connection with what precedes and thinks them a fragment or part of another psalm; Ellicott grants the abruptness but holds that omniscience must lead the mind to the existence of evil, and that the Hebrew, unlike a modern, turned not to speculation about the origin of evil but to indignation at sin in concrete act; Keil and Delitzsch make the same connection in an exclamation that this God is by many hated and blasphemed.

How is the hatred of the closing verses to be taken? Wesley disposes of it in a line as the difference between the Jewish and the Christian spirit; Gill narrows it to men as haters of God and to their works rather than their persons, the Gospel requiring love and prayer for them as creatures; Clarke abhors their conduct, motives and purposes; Ellicott turns it into a question and compares a phrase of Tennyson.

What is to be made of the twentieth verse? Clarke reports a bishop’s rendering about men sworn to a rash purpose, says he cannot see these things in the original, and prefers the reading followed by almost all the older versions in which the wicked seize upon God’s cities; Ellicott calls the text unsatisfactory, doubts rendering enemies a word that properly means cities, cites two Greek translators giving rivals and adversaries, and adopts a change of pointing for the first clause and the simplest emendation for the second.
outliers: Clarke observes that the psalmist needed such a prayer as the closing one just because he was filled with indignation, since he who utterly hates the practices of any man is not far from hating the man himself, and quotes a couplet on the difficulty of hating the sin with all the heart and yet loving the sinner.

Clarke cites a bishop distinguishing two Hebrew words for way, one being the right way in which a man ought to go and the other the way, right or wrong, in which he actually goes by habit, and adds that the way right in a man’s own eyes is seldom the way to God.
Spurgeon has the psalmist chase the men of blood from his court, saying in effect that if God will not let them live with him he will not have them live with him either.
themes: a closing section suspected of belonging elsewhere
omniscience issuing in a demand for judgment
hatred narrowed to conduct and disowned outright
a corrupt verse repaired three different ways
the opening confession turned into a closing petition
